title: Arrays and Objects
subtitle: Organize collections of information using arrays and objects.
description: Learn how to create, access and manipulate arrays and objects and understand how structured data works.

blocks.text: Welcome to Lesson 7: Arrays and Objects. This lesson follows the course dashboard topic “Arrays and Objects”. The goal is to organize collections of information using arrays and objects.. Focus on understanding when this technique is useful, what assumptions it makes, and how you can check that it is working.
Collections group related values. Use a sequence when order or position matters, a set when uniqueness is the main concern, and a map or dictionary when values should be found by a meaningful key.

blocks.question: A list contains a value at the first position. In a zero-based language, which index usually addresses it?
options: One.
The collection length.
Zero.
Minus one.
blocks.explanation: Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Most common programming-language arrays and lists use zero-based indexing, though language-specific structures may differ.

blocks.question: A collection must contain each category only once. What data structure or operation helps?
options: A list that intentionally keeps every duplicate.
A set or explicit uniqueness check.
A loop that prints the items.
A longer variable name.
blocks.explanation: A set or uniqueness rule prevents repeated categories.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. A set or uniqueness rule prevents repeated categories.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. A set or uniqueness rule prevents repeated categories.

blocks.text: Indexes are commonly zero-based, so the first element is often at position zero and the last index is one less than the collection length. Key-based collections use keys instead of numeric positions and may have different lookup guarantees.

blocks.question: A collection lookup can fail when the key is missing. What should the code do?
options: Check for absence or use a documented fallback/error result.
Assume every possible key exists.
Use the missing value as a list index.
Ignore the result and display success.
blocks.explanation: Handling absent keys makes the behavior predictable and avoids hidden failures.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Handling absent keys makes the behavior predictable and avoids hidden failures.
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Review the requirement again. Handling absent keys makes the behavior predictable and avoids hidden failures.

blocks.question: A program repeatedly looks up a learner by a unique email address. Which structure is a natural fit?
options: A map/dictionary keyed by email, with suitable uniqueness handling.
A random number with no mapping.
A paragraph of comma-separated values that is never parsed.
A loop that guesses the correct person.
blocks.explanation: Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
blocks.hint: Identify the requirement in the scenario, eliminate choices that ignore it, and choose the option that preserves correctness and maintainability.
blocks.correctFeedback: Correct. Key-value structures express lookup by identifier more directly than repeatedly scanning unrelated data.
